title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration versus plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc sensitivity quantification tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of operator intent into device configuration promises faster NetOps workflows but raises operational risk when generated changes are misordered, incomplete, or unsafe. Recent literature recommends generate→verify→repair designs that pair probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic validators or simulators as floor‑safety nets. Despite these proposals and small‑scale demos, there are few preregistered, paired A/B experiments that quantify how a bounded guarded pipeline affects first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics.

This study implements a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment that evaluates a minimal guarded pipeline: a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot), a frozen deterministic validator performing rule and dependency checks, and at most one automated repair attempt when the validator detects violations. Our core research question is: Can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (1) a preregistered confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic seed generation and archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces; (2) confirmatory statistics showing a near‑ceiling baseline and a single corrected discordance; (3) a short post‑hoc inferential sensitivity analysis grounded in the archived contingency counts; (4) operational recommendations for calibrating task difficulty and repair budgets in future confirmatory NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Surveys and system papers show LLMs can synthesize configuration templates or translate intent into device commands in controlled settings, but they also document failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety. Cross‑domain results in medical QA and code generation demonstrate that retrieval augmentation, deterministic verifiers, and bounded repair loops reduce factual errors and improve grounding; NetOps architectural proposals repeatedly recommend deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets and generate→verify→repair pipelines for agentic workflows. However, few works provide preregistered, paired A/B experiments using deterministically generated task banks, frozen validators, and bounded repair budgets. Our experiment situates itself at this intersection: a tightly constrained, preregistered confirmatory test of a minimal guarded pipeline with full artifact archival.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study preregistration (id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) froze the design before execution. Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations was a baseline pass rate = 0.40 (see preregistration id for archived planning details). The preregistered sampling, analysis, and retry policies were fixed prior to observing outcomes.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministically generated seeds from the frozen task generator. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics) was used for both arms: baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the same candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The choice to share the initial candidate was preregistered and materially affects within‑pair correlation and the number of informative discordant pairs available for McNemar inference. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Model, validator, and scoring: The declared model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter (validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implements rule‑ and dependency‑based checks, canonicalizes configurations to normalized ASTs, and emits binary pass/fail scoring together with violation codes used for repair decisions. Scoring semantics apply a full intent‑constraint validation: an output is scored as a success only when the validator deems required command sequences and dependency constraints satisfied. The experiment treated model/provider failures according to the preregistered missingness plan (one retry allowed; primary analysis treatment 'complete_pair_primary' drops pairs only if both calls fail).

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired pass/fail outcomes. We report the absolute risk difference with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed fixed) as prespecified. Secondary analyses include repair success rate with exact binomial intervals and sensitivity checks for missingness and contamination. All analysis code and per‑task artifacts were archived; the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle enumerate the archived items.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301; a single repair‑stage model call was invoked under the preregistered repair budget. No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the retry policy; the contingency accounting is complete under the preregistered reconciliation checks.

Primary outcomes (artifact‑derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency: n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). These counts are produced directly from the archived contingency summary in the analysis artifact bundle and were used for confirmatory inference.

Statistical inference: Applying the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test to the observed contingency yields p = 1.00. The observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729), as archived in the analysis outputs. Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole initially invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); the exact Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 is [0.025, 1.0], reflecting wide uncertainty given a single observed repair case.

Post‑hoc sensitivity and interpretive bound: The observed discordant pair total (n10 + n01 = 1) imposes a hard resolution limit on the absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the point estimate). With only a single discordant pair the two‑sided exact McNemar calculation yields p = 1.00 for the symmetric null because the test is driven by discordant counts; one discordance provides insufficient evidence to reject the null of no paired difference. The bootstrap CI upper bound (0.01) bounds plausible absolute improvement under the run's sampling semantics. By construction, the preregistered target (≈+0.30 absolute corresponding to a 50% relative reduction from the assumed baseline) is orders of magnitude larger than the resolvable improvement in this run; the observed near‑ceiling baseline therefore invalidates the preregistered power assumption and precludes confirmatory support for H1.

Representative artifact diagnostics: Per‑task validator traces show the validator's normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flags for every episode. The single baseline failure resolved by repair was corrected by applying the preregistered repair prompt/adapter and revalidating; the guard showed a final normalized_configuration that satisfied the intent constraints per the deterministic validator. For reproducibility, the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle enumerate all per‑task normalized responses, validator decisions, and repair traces; readers are directed to those archived artifacts (see Disclosure Statement) rather than to inline run bookkeeping in the text.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the lone invalid baseline output, demonstrating that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, the experiment does not provide evidence for the preregistered large effect (≥50% relative reduction) because the empirical baseline pass rate was far higher than assumed. Two pragmatic lessons follow.

First, difficulty calibration matters for confirmatory NetOps experiments. To detect substantial absolute improvements, designers must ensure the task bank produces a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence. Options include adversarially augmenting tasks, increasing task difficulty, or targeting estimands conditional on initial failure (e.g., repair conditional efficacy) rather than population‑level absolute reduction. We recommend preregistering target initial‑failure counts (not only sample size) so that power calculations directly map to the number of informative discordant pairs expected under paired semantics.

Second, pairing semantics and repair budgets affect inferential power and operational realism. Reusing a shared initial candidate per pair reduces the number of informative discordant pairs relative to independent draws; independent draws increase discordance potential but add cross‑arm heterogeneity. The preregistered choice to share candidates increased within‑pair correlation and thus reduced detectable differences for a given N. Likewise, restricting repair to a single automated iteration bounds operational realism; production guardrails often permit multiple automated repair attempts and human review. Future confirmatory studies should preregister pairing semantics, desired initial‑failure counts, and realistic repair budgets aligned with the operational claim being tested.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the shared_initial_candidate design choice (preregistered). Construct validity is limited because the deterministic validator evaluates canonicalized configuration and constraint satisfaction rather than executing configurations in a live network; runtime packet‑level reachability or performance effects were not measured. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, the constrained vendor‑template space, a single model family (gpt-5-mini), and a single validator implementation. Conclusion validity is constrained by the small number of informative discordant pairs; statistical inference about large preregistered effects is therefore not supported by the observed data.

Recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps experiments: (1) preregister target counts of initial failures (not only N) and calibrate task banks to achieve them; (2) explicitly preregister pairing semantics and report their impact on expected discordant counts for power calculations; (3) when operational claims require runtime assurances, incorporate emulation/simulation steps that exercise packet‑level or control‑plane consequences rather than relying solely on static configuration validators; (4) treat repair success as a conditioned estimand (conditional on initial failure) when baseline pass rates are uncertain.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) using a frozen deterministic validator and a one‑iteration automated repair budget applied to gpt‑5‑mini outputs, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs. The single automated repair corrected the only observed invalid baseline output, but the run does not support the preregistered claim of ≥50% relative reduction in misconfiguration because the observed baseline contradicted the planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and left no statistical headroom. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should calibrate task difficulty to produce sufficient initial failures, preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly, and measure runtime semantic effects via emulation when operational claims are required. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.
The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicts that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
